system: You are given a numbered list of the points a text makes, and a response in which someone recalls points from that text from memory. Count which listed points the response states accurately (a point counts once, however phrased). Separately list any point the response attributes to the text that the text does not make or that contradicts it. Reply with JSON only: {"recalled": [point numbers], "inaccurate": ["..."]}
message:
POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
From memory, so the wording is approximate and I may have some details wrong:

**Opening**
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in the day, or when a team is new.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a weight. Part comes from the evidence and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim and how closely. Conclusions from people who've worked in an area for years have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, since it reflects checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports the defect rate fell after a process change. Take it as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Make sure you've taken in a paper, message or review, and show it. Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This isn't politeness; it keeps a conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, and extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement puts people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- Example: a manager's five-point request has the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms direction, picks up what you can act on now, and says the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material. A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and can't act.
- Example: the notes say a report found "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions are settled and some less certain. Mark which is which, then keep moving.
- Open questions block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited; a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping questions open because one more check feels safer, is more common in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- Once the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan rollout, including the busiest site with a different workflow, handling problems as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues, and colleagues from elsewhere in the organisation, see things differently, which is valuable only if their time goes where it's useful. A reviewer starting from scratch spends most effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- When asking someone to check your work, give context: what you concluded, where the risks are, and what to focus on.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- You'll often see a good next step. First check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind: share drafts with the lead, confirm direction before making the call, release when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked, which costs more than a short conversation would have.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps don't need sign-off, but most steps that matter affect others, so check first and act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether and how they'd like it restructured.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other. The pairs:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing
  - Inventing a flaw / overlooking one
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long
  - Abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively. The latter is defined as disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
  - Acting alone / waiting too long
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, which you'll mostly carry without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records, an agreed direction. Trust those; they're how good work gets done together.

I'm least sure of the exact wording throughout, the precise phrasing of some pair definitions in §7, and the exact list in §6 ("share drafts… make the call… release the result").
